reading.title: Ἀπὸ Σάρδεων διὰ Φρυγίας
reading.audioPlaceholder: Reading audio has not yet been recorded.
introduction: The expedition resumes. This reading selects connected moments from the march: a river crossing, the stay at Celaenae, further contingents, the games at Peltae, and overdue pay at Caystru-pedion.

Source: Xenophon, Anabasis 1.2.5–11 supplies the itinerary, bridge, places, gathering, games, and arrears. Xenophon as our observing viewpoint, ordinary soldiers’ remarks, and descriptive transitions are course reconstruction. We do not translate the full itinerary or invent a witnessed conversation for the ancient author.

Adapted present-tense Attic Greek gives the first formal practice in present middle participles. These forms describe people traveling, preparing, and receiving; blue glosses support place names, numbers, and other constructions not yet assessed.

paragraphs.greek: Ὁ Κῦρος ἀπὸ Σάρδεων πορεύεται, καὶ ἡ στρατιὰ διὰ τῆς Λυδίας βαδίζει. οἱ πορευόμενοι τὰ ὅπλα φέρουσιν. ὁ Ξενοφῶν μετὰ τοῦ Προξένου τὴν ὁδὸν σκοπεῖ.
Ἡ στρατιὰ πρὸς τὸν Μαίανδρον ἀφικνεῖται. ἐπὶ τοῦ ποταμοῦ γέφυρα ἐκ πλοίων ἐστίν. οἱ στρατιῶται ἐπὶ τῆς γεφύρας βαδίζουσιν· οἱ παρασκευαζόμενοι τὰ ὅπλα καὶ τὰ χρήματα φυλάττουσιν.
Ἐν Φρυγίᾳ ἡ στρατιὰ πρὸς Κολοσσὰς πορεύεται, ἔπειτα δὲ εἰς Κελαινὰς ἀφικνεῖται. ἐνταῦθα ὁ Κῦρος οἰκήματα καὶ παράδεισον ἔχει. ὁ Μαίανδρος διὰ τοῦ παραδείσου ῥεῖ.
Ἄλλα στρατεύματα πρὸς Κῦρον ἔρχονται. ὁ Κλέαρχος ὁπλίτας καὶ πελταστὰς καὶ τοξότας ἄγει. οἱ στρατιῶται οἱ παρασκευαζόμενοι ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ εἰσίν, καὶ ὁ Κῦρος τὴν στρατιὰν ἐξετάζει.

reading.translation:
Cyrus travels from Sardis, and the army marches through Lydia. Those traveling carry their weapons. Xenophon examines the route with Proxenus.

The army arrives at the Maeander. Over the river is a bridge made of boats. The soldiers walk over the bridge; those preparing keep watch over weapons and resources.

In Phrygia the army travels to Colossae and then arrives at Celaenae. There Cyrus has buildings and a park. The Maeander flows through the park.

Other contingents come to Cyrus. Clearchus leads hoplites, peltasts, and archers. The soldiers who are preparing are in the park, and Cyrus reviews the army.

While traveling, Xenophon sees his friends. The friends discuss the route: “The army uses extensive preparation,” they say. Others prepare their own belongings.

The army arrives at Peltae. Xenias prepares a sacrifice and games in honor of Lycaean Zeus. The athletes compete, and Cyrus watches the games. Golden strigils are the prizes.

Those competing make their friends rejoice, but the soldiers also ask for pay. They arrive at Caystru-pedion. There Cyrus owes more than three months’ pay.

The soldiers repeatedly come to Cyrus and ask for their pay. Cyrus speaks of hopes, but the money is not yet available. Xenophon sees the soldiers’ effort; those marching need food and pay.

wordStudy.label: Word Study — Travel, Contests, and Pay

blocks.title: Words in the Reading
body: πορεύομαι gives πορευόμενος, “traveling.” παρασκευάζομαι gives παρασκευαζόμενος, “preparing.” The form names a participant in an ongoing action, and its adjective-like ending lets it describe a specific person.

ἀγών is a contest; ἀγωνίζομαι means compete; ἀγωνιζόμενος is a person competing. The word family connects the games at Peltae to the participants. The middle form translates naturally as an active English action.
μισθός is pay, not a prize. ἆθλον is a contest prize. Cyrus’s soldiers can enjoy games and still need overdue wages: the vocabulary keeps these different kinds of payment distinct.

grammar.intro: Present middle participle formation, declension, deponents, uses, and relative time. Work through each section, use its checks and topic practice, then complete the grammar exercises. Reading-only forms remain supported by glosses.
objectives: Form present middle participles, including familiar contracted forms.
Decline participles and match gender, number, and case to their referents.
Translate deponent participles by their lexical meanings.
Interpret attributive, substantival, and simple circumstantial uses.
Relate ongoing participial action to a finite main action and preserve participants when recasting a clause.

sections.title: 1. Forming Present Middle Participles
body: Take the present stem and add -όμενος, -ομένη, -όμενον: πορευ- becomes πορευόμενος, πορευομένη, πορευόμενον. These are masculine, feminine, and neuter nominative singular forms. A participle is a verbal adjective; it is not a finite personal ending such as -εται.
The present participle represents an ongoing action. παρασκευαζόμενος is preparing, and ἀγωνιζόμενος is competing. Accent is part of the form: masculine/neuter -όμενος/-όμενον and feminine -ομένη.

Familiar alpha-contract verbs contract the connecting vowel: θεαόμενος → θεώμενος, “watching”; τιμαόμενος → τιμώμενος, “honoring for oneself” or “being honored,” according to voice and context. Learn familiar contract forms with their verbs rather than assigning a fixed English passive to every middle form.

checks.answer: No. It is a participle, and needs a noun/referent and a finite clause for a full sentence.

sections.title: 2. Declension and Agreement
body: Middle participles decline like first/second-declension adjectives. Masculine/neuter use second-declension endings, feminine uses the first-declension -η pattern. Their gender, number, and case agree with the person or thing described.

Compare ὁ πορευόμενος στρατιώτης, subject singular, with τοὺς πορευομένους στρατιώτας, object plural. The ending tells you which noun the participle belongs to; it does not change who does the traveling.

When several nouns appear, match the participle’s ending to its referent before translating. In ὁ Κῦρος τοὺς πορευομένους στρατιώτας ὁρᾷ, the soldiers travel and Cyrus sees. Agreement prevents attributing both actions to Cyrus.

examples.greek: ὁ Κῦρος τοὺς πορευομένους στρατιώτας ὁρᾷ.

examples.english: He brings food to the friends who are preparing.

checks.prompt: Who travels in Cyrus’s seeing sentence?
checks.answer: The soldiers, because πορευομένους agrees with στρατιώτας.

sections.title: 3. Participles of Deponents
body: Deponents such as πορεύομαι and ἀγωνίζομαι use middle present forms with active lexical meanings. Their participles keep those meanings: πορευόμενος, traveling; ἀγωνιζόμενος, competing. Do not translate them as “being traveled” or “being competed.”

Other familiar examples include βουλόμενος, wanting; δεχόμενος, receiving; διαλεγόμενος, conversing. Each describes the action of the person it agrees with. παρασκευαζόμενος can emphasize preparing one’s own equipment or preparing oneself in context.

Voice comes from the verb’s meaning and construction, not an isolated ending. A middle/passive participle of another verb can have a passive interpretation. Today’s taught examples focus on familiar deponents and middle preparation.

checks.answer: No. It means competing, from the deponent ἀγωνίζομαι.

sections.title: 4. Describing, Naming, and Accompanying
body: Attributive participles describe a noun inside an article group: οἱ πορευόμενοι στρατιῶται, “the traveling soldiers.” The second attributive position repeats the article: οἱ στρατιῶται οἱ πορευόμενοι. Both identify the soldiers by their action.

A substantival participle has the article without an expressed noun: οἱ πορευόμενοι, “those traveling.” As with substantive adjectives, the context supplies the people or things. A participle may still take an object, as ὁ δεχόμενος τὸν μισθόν, “the person receiving the pay.”

A simple circumstantial participle accompanies the main action without being enclosed in its article group: ὁ Ξενοφῶν πορευόμενος τοὺς φίλους ὁρᾷ, “while traveling, Xenophon sees his friends.” Here while fits the context. Do not automatically impose because or although when the sentence supplies no such relationship.

checks.prompt: What has been omitted in οἱ πορευόμενοι?
checks.answer: An expressed noun such as soldiers; the participle itself names the group.

sections.title: 5. Ongoing Action and Relative Time
body: A present participle describes ongoing action relative to the main verb. It does not independently assign a calendar date. Our story’s main verbs are in the present, so πορευόμενος ὁρᾷ means “while traveling, he sees.”

Keep the same participant when converting a simple clause: ὁ Ξενοφῶν πορεύεται καὶ τοὺς φίλους ὁρᾷ → ὁ Ξενοφῶν πορευόμενος τοὺς φίλους ὁρᾷ. This presents his ongoing traveling as accompanying his seeing. It does not create a new traveler.

Participles are not personal verbs. πορευόμενος alone does not say “he travels” as a complete clause. Find the finite verb, establish its subject, then connect the agreeing participle. In a past narrative a present participle would still describe ongoing action relative to that past main action; the past forms themselves are not today’s exercise target.

checks.prompt: Does the present participle itself establish that the event is happening today?
checks.answer: No; its ongoing action is interpreted relative to the main action.

summary.title: Grammar Summary
items: Present middle participles use -όμενος, -ομένη, -όμενον; familiar contract vowels contract.
First/second-declension endings give agreement with a noun or contextual referent.
A deponent participle can have an active English meaning: ἀγωνιζόμενος, competing.
An article group describes or names; a circumstantial participle accompanies the main action.
Present participles present ongoing relative action and do not independently establish calendar time.

culture.title: Marching, Royal Parks, and Overdue Wages

sections.title: Reading an itinerary as human movement
body: Anabasis 1.2.5–11 records stages, distances, stopping places, and the arrival of further forces. The boat bridge over the Maeander is an example of practical infrastructure that lets an army move. Our reading selects the crossing and a few stopping places to make the journey manageable rather than asking beginners to reproduce the full numerical itinerary.

The road runs through Lydia into Phrygia. These are named regions in Xenophon’s account, not interchangeable labels for all of Asia. Travel joins geography to material tasks: carrying equipment, watching possessions, and arranging food. The ordinary conversations in our reading are reconstructed examples, while the named route and bridge are source-based.

sections.title: A park and a festival on campaign
body: At Celaenae Xenophon describes Cyrus’s palace and a large hunting park, with the Maeander flowing through it. Additional contingents gather, and Cyrus reviews the Greeks there. The park belongs to the royal environment of the march; παράδεισος here does not mean an afterlife paradise. Geography, royal resources, and military assembly meet at this stop.

At Peltae Xenias celebrates a festival for Lycaean Zeus with sacrifice and athletic games. Cyrus watches, and golden strigils are awarded as prizes. A strigil is the curved implement used to scrape oil and dirt from the body. The festival brings familiar Greek athletic and religious activity into the expedition without making the journey itself a holiday.

sections.title: Pay as a condition of cooperation
body: By Caystru-pedion the troops are owed more than three months’ wages. Xenophon reports repeated requests for payment and Cyrus’s expressions of hope. The amount in arrears matters: these men depend on resources, and promises alone do not remove their needs. Their pressure is part of the expedition’s practical story.

Our distinction between μισθός, pay, and ἆθλον, prize, helps avoid treating rewards at games as a substitute for wages. The next lesson follows Epyaxa’s arrival and the payment of four months’ wages. A question for reflection is how a leader can secure cooperation when the material obligations that support it remain unmet.

questions.prompt: What practical feature helps the army cross the Maeander?
What does παράδεισος mean at Celaenae?

questions.answer: Xenias, in honor of Lycaean Zeus.

questions.prompt: What are the prizes at the games?
How much pay is overdue at Caystru-pedion?
Why distinguish a prize from pay?
questions.answer: Athletic prizes do not satisfy the army’s ordinary wage obligations.

items: Present middle participles use -όμενος, -ομένη, -όμενον; familiar contract vowels contract.
First/second-declension endings give agreement with a noun or contextual referent.
A deponent participle can have an active English meaning: ἀγωνιζόμενος, competing.
An article group describes or names; a circumstantial participle accompanies the main action.
